newsitem.title: USA: CSCE coffee slumps to end at one-month low.
newsitem.headline: CSCE coffee slumps to end at one-month low.

text.p: CSCE coffee prices tumbled Wednesday to their lowest level in a month, battered by waning supply concerns and news of impending reduction to speculative position limits on the Exchange's "C" coffee contract, trading sources said..

The Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange said early in the day it planned to slash the speculative position limit from 500 to 200 lots for contracts in notice (delivery) period. The change, which is subject to approval by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), would take effect with the December 1996 contract.
Traders said the move is aimed at reducing volatility on the spot month after market operators complained of squeeze plays on the July and September 1996 contracts.

Although speculators have some two months to clear their books of excess positions before the December contract enters notice period, the news sparked a bout of panic selling early in the session, traders said. Automatic sell orders were triggered below 109.10 and 108.50, compounding the downward momentum.
Benchmark December fell 4.40 cents a lb on the day, to settle at 106.90, just off their intraday or of 106.50.
Selling was broad-based, as typically bargain-hungry processors stood clear.
Analysts said that while the new position limit may have sparked this morning's selling frenzy, the imminent arrival of new-crop coffee to consuming markets made the downturn inevitable.
"The flow of coffee is going to increase in the weeks ahead, it's not going to decline," said Smith Barney analyst Walter Spilka. "The fundamentals are shifting negative."
December's failure to hold above 110 cents, a key psychological level, confirmed the bearish trend for many speculators, he said.
Consistently favorable growing conditions in Brazil had dashed bulls' hopes for another rally on the expiring September contract, said Merrill Lynch analyst Judith Ganes.
"Brazil has had a pretty good start to the rainy season," she said. "Concerns about tight delivery are over."
Prices would likely test the 100.00 cent ($1) level before stabilizing between 90-110 cents per lb, she said.
The day's volume was estimated at a hefty 12,308 lots.
-- Wendy Pollack, New York Commodities Desk +1 212 859 1640
